title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
description: Truth and deception, family and trust, independence and bravery, neurodiversity — plus Eduqas exam.
content_html:
Theme 1: Truth and Deception

The most pervasive theme in Stephens's play is the tension between Christopher's absolute commitment to truth and the adults around him who deceive him in the name of love. 'I do not tell lies' is Christopher's defining principle — yet he lives in a world constructed almost entirely from lies. Ed lied about Judy dying. Ed lied about killing Wellington. The entire domestic reality of Act 1 is a fiction.

Stephens presents this tension without simple moral resolution. Ed's lies are motivated by love, not malice. He believed — wrongly — that his version of reality would protect Christopher from pain. The play shows that this kind of protective deception is ultimately more harmful than the truth would have been: Christopher's response to learning his father has lied is not grief but logical deduction that his father might harm him. The architecture of lies collapses into danger rather than safety.

Key Fact

The central irony: Ed lies to protect Christopher, but because Christopher values truth absolutely ('I do not tell lies'), the discovery of the lies is uniquely destructive — more damaging than the truth would have been. Love expressed through deception becomes a form of harm.

Theme 2: Family, Trust, and Broken Relationships

The play presents a family that has failed in multiple directions simultaneously. Ed's marriage collapsed; Judy left Christopher and moved to London; Ed rebuilt a partial relationship with Mrs Shears which also collapsed. Christopher exists at the centre of these adult failures, protected from them by lies but shaped by the absences they create.

Stephens does not present family restoration as straightforwardly possible. At the end of the play, Christopher has shared custody between Ed and Judy. This is not the recovery of a nuclear family but a functional arrangement that acknowledges what has broken and what remains. The play's treatment of family is honest and uncomfortable: love is real, damage is real, and both persist simultaneously.

Christopher's relationships with Ed and Judy are both complex and asymmetric. Ed is consistently present — even when he lies, he is there, managing, protecting, doing what he can. Judy is absent, then suddenly present, overwhelmed by guilt. Both relationships are shaped by Christopher's additional needs: Ed's deception partly reflects the exhaustion of single parenting; Judy's departure partly reflects the difficulty of that same challenge. Stephens presents both parents as struggling with something genuinely hard, rather than condemning either of them. The play asks the audience to hold complexity: to see the damage and the love at once.

Theme 3: Independence and Bravery

Christopher's journey to London is the play's central act of bravery. He has never travelled independently. The journey subjects him to everything he finds most difficult — crowds, unpredictability, sensory overload — and he survives it, finds his mother, and returns. The theatrical staging of the journey (Frantic Assembly's choreography, the ensemble as crowd) makes the scale of this achievement physically present for the audience.

The play frames bravery in Christopher's own terms. He does not experience the journey as heroic — he experiences it as terrifying. But he does it anyway, step by step, because the logic of his situation demands it. His bravery is not the instinctive courage of a conventional protagonist; it is the determined, methodical persistence of a person who continues because the alternative — not knowing — is worse. This is a distinctive form of bravery that the play invites the audience to recognise and admire.

Key Fact

Christopher's bravery is methodical and determined rather than instinctive. He does not feel brave — he feels terrified. But he continues because the logic of his situation demands it. The play invites the audience to recognise this as a form of courage that neurotypical frameworks often miss.

Theme 4: Neurodiversity and the Challenge to the Deficit Model

Stephens's play consistently presents Christopher's neurodivergent way of experiencing the world as the audience's primary reality. His literal language, his logical deduction, his mathematical precision, his need for predictable routine — these are not presented as limitations to be overcome but as characteristics that produce both exceptional capability and genuine vulnerability. The play challenges the audience to recognise that the neurotypical world — its ambiguity, its use of social lies, its non-verbal codes — is just as difficult and arbitrary as it feels to Christopher.

For AO4 (context), students should engage with the theatrical and cultural context of the 2012 National Theatre premiere. Writing for a 2012 audience, adapting a 2003 novel, Stephens continued Haddon's challenge to the deficit model of autism. The play-within-a-play structure, in which the audience inhabits Christopher's perspective throughout, is a theatrical embodiment of this challenge: the audience sees the world as Christopher does, not as the neurotypical adults do.

Key Quotations for the Eduqas Exam

The following quotations are reliably attested in the play-text and are appropriate for the Eduqas exam. All are framed as play quotations, not novel quotations:

'I do not tell lies.' — Christopher's core principle. Use to analyse his character's relationship to truth and why deception is uniquely damaging to him.

'I find people confusing.' — Christopher's explanation of his social difficulties. Use to analyse his relationship to language and communication.

'I am not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different... maybe if you'd been different... but that is not your fault.' — Judy's letter. Use to analyse Judy's character, the theme of parental failure, and the complexity of responsibility.

'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' — Christopher on mathematics. Use to analyse his relationship to certainty and the symbolism of mathematics.

'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — The play's final question. Use to analyse the ending, the question vs declaration distinction, and Siobhan's significance as the person whose answer matters most.

'Siobhan understands. When she tells me not to do something she tells me exactly what it is I am not allowed to do. I like this.' — Christopher on Siobhan. Use to analyse his relationship with her and the theme of clear communication.

Key Fact

Core play quotations: 'I do not tell lies' (truth/character); 'I find people confusing' (communication); 'that is not your fault' (family/Judy); 'Prime numbers... patterns away' (mathematics/certainty); 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' (ending/independence); Siobhan understands (trust/communication).

Exam Technique: Writing About a Play

The your written exam question gives you a short extract from the play and asks you to analyse it and the play as a whole. The question is worth 40 marks (35 for quality + 5 for accuracy and ambition in spelling, punctuation, and vocabulary).

A strong response will: attribute craft choices to 'Stephens' not 'Haddon'; analyse theatrical devices as well as language; embed AO4 context naturally (2012 National Theatre premiere, the challenge to the deficit model, Stephens's adaptation of Haddon); range across the whole play; and use precisely worded quotations from the play-text.

For AO4, include context about the play, not just the novel. Useful AO4 points include: Stephens's 2012 adaptation for the National Theatre, directed by Marianne Elliott; the production's use of Frantic Assembly's physical theatre to embody Christopher's sensory experience; the seven Olivier Awards and five Tony Awards (indicating the play's cultural significance and reach); the challenge to the deficit model of autism in both 2003 (Haddon's novel) and 2012 (Stephens's play). The novel's Whitbread Award is useful background context, but it is the play's theatrical context that is directly relevant for AO4 in the Eduqas exam.

Example AO4 sentence: 'Adapting Haddon's 2003 novel for the National Theatre in 2012, Stephens uses Siobhan's co-narration to present Christopher's perspective directly to the audience, challenging the deficit model of autism by making Christopher's logical and mathematical way of experiencing the world the primary lens through which the audience understands events.'

Model Analytical Paragraph

Here is a model paragraph demonstrating how to write about the Stephens play at a high level:

'Stephens presents Christopher's relationship with truth as both his greatest strength and his greatest vulnerability. His declaration 'I do not tell lies' establishes an absolute moral standard that the play's adult world consistently fails to meet, creating a sustained dramatic irony in which the audience comes to recognise Christopher's truthfulness as more ethically consistent than the neurotypical deceptions that surround him. The theatrical effect of the play-within-a-play structure is to align the audience with Christopher's perspective: as Siobhan reads his account, we understand what the adults do not. When Ed's lies are revealed in Act 2, Christopher's logical deduction — that if Father has lied, Father might harm him — is presented not as a symptom of his neurodivergence but as a rational response to available evidence. Stephens uses Christopher's literal logic to expose the self-deception in Ed's protective dishonesty, suggesting that love without honesty is ultimately a form of harm.'

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas exam, always write 'Stephens presents' not 'Haddon presents'. Never mention chapters — use 'the play', 'Act 1', 'Act 2', 'the scene'. Always refer to the play's ending correctly: Christopher asks Siobhan 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' — a question, not the novel's declarative 'I can do anything'. When embedding AO4 context, prioritise the 2012 theatrical context (National Theatre premiere, Frantic Assembly, Olivier/Tony Awards) alongside the novel's 2003 background.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The central irony of the truth/deception theme: Ed's protective lies are more harmful than the truth would have been, because Christopher's literal commitment to honesty makes deception uniquely destructive.
  • The play ends with Christopher asking Siobhan a question ('Does that mean I can do anything?') — not the novel's declaration. This is the most important single distinction for the Eduqas exam.
  • AO4 context must reference the play: 2012 National Theatre premiere, Marianne Elliott, Frantic Assembly, seven Olivier Awards, Stephens's adaptation choices.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present the theme of truth and deception in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the central irony: Ed's protective deception is uniquely harmful to Christopher because of his absolute commitment to truth. Discusses: 'I do not tell lies', the interconnected web of Ed's lies, Christopher's logical response to the confession, Judy's letters and her admission ('I am not a very good mother... that is not your fault'), Siobhan's contrasting honesty. Range across both acts.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with sustained evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response engaging with the theme.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some relevant points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens explore the theme of family in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the play's complex treatment of family. Discusses: Ed's love and deception as simultaneous, Judy's absence and guilt ('I am not a very good mother'), the discovery of the letters as the moment the false family is exposed, the shared custody as honest rather than restored resolution. AO4: challenges of family under pressure; single parenting of a child with additional needs.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present independence and bravery through Christopher's journey in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Christopher's distinctive bravery: methodical, terrified, determined. Discusses the theatrical staging of the journey (ensemble as sensory overload), Toby's rescue, the arrival in London, and the connection between the journey and the final question ('Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'). What does the play suggest about bravery for a neurodivergent person?
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the play to challenge attitudes towards neurodiversity?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of how the play's form embeds the challenge to the deficit model. Discusses: the play-within-a-play making Christopher's perspective the audience's primary reality, his literal logic as morally consistent, his mathematical precision as a form of excellence, and the way the neurotypical world (ambiguity, lies, non-verbal codes) is presented as strange from Christopher's viewpoint. AO4: 2012 theatrical context, neurodiversity discourse.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with AO4 embedded.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use Siobhan's final role in the play to bring together the themes of trust, communication, and independence?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the final scene as convergence of themes. Siobhan's trustworthiness (established through precise communication throughout) makes her the right person for Christopher to ask his final question. Her co-narrator role means she has been present at every moment of the play — she has witnessed everything. Christopher asking her 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' brings together the trust theme (who can Christopher rely on?), the communication theme (who communicates honestly with him?), and the independence theme (what has he proved about himself?).
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present the ending of the play as both hopeful and uncertain?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of the ending's tonal complexity. Hopeful: the A* result, the question to Siobhan, the tentative reconciliation with Ed, the gift of Sandy. Uncertain: the question is unanswered, the family is not restored, the relationship with Ed requires rebuilding. Discusses the question form as theatrically open (contrasts with the novel's declarative certainty). AO2: what the question vs declaration distinction means for meaning and audience response.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis of both tones.
Mid band (15-21): Some engagement with complexity.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the central irony of the truth/deception theme?
options: Christopher lies to protect his father, but Ed discovers the truth anyway
Judy is honest but Christopher doesn't believe her
Ed's protective lies are more harmful than the truth would have been, because Christopher values truth absolutely
The detective investigation reveals that Christopher is the real cause of the family's problems

knowledge_checks.q: Which quotation correctly represents the play's ending — not the novel's?
options: 'And that means I can do anything.'
'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'
'I know I can do this because I went to London on my own.'
'I solved the mystery of Who Killed Wellington?'

knowledge_checks.q: Christopher says: 'I do not tell _____.' — his defining moral principle.

Match each key quotation to its thematic relevance:
left: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away'
'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?'
right: Truth and deception — Christopher's absolute commitment to honesty makes Ed's lies uniquely damaging
Mathematics and certainty — Christopher's language of clarity and precision in an ambiguous world
Independence and the ending — aspiration rather than certainty, directed to the one person Christopher trusts

flashcard_questions.a: Truth and deception; family and broken trust; independence and bravery; neurodiversity and the challenge to the deficit model.

glossary_terms.definition: A model that views neurological difference as a disorder requiring correction — the play challenges this by presenting Christopher's logical way of experiencing the world as the audience's primary reality.

Assessment Objective 4 — showing understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written, performed, and received. For this play, AO4 should reference the 2012 theatrical context.
When the audience knows something a character does not — the play generates dramatic irony by showing the audience, through Siobhan's narration, what Christopher understands and what he misses.

The development of a theme through the course of the play — the truth/deception theme arcs from Act 1 (the lies in place) through Act 2 (the collapse of the lies) to the ending (what remains after the truth).
A sentence that asks a question — the form of the play's final line, distinguishing it from the novel's declarative certainty and creating an open, aspirational ending.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
The sense of anticipation or unease created by conflict, uncertainty, or approaching crisis in drama.
A recurring image, symbol, or idea in a text that carries thematic significance.
